title: San Francisco Power Grid Experiences Micro-Blackouts Traced to Single Terminal
subtitle: 340 outages, each under two seconds, all tracing back to one residential address with a load signature engineers say “looks like a whole building, not a person.”
excerpt: “We have never had a single apartment unit request a load profile that looks like this.” PG&E has installed a dedicated regulator “as a precaution.”
author: By Marcus Feld
heroHTML:
GRID: PG&E SECTOR 14

EVENTS: 340 | SOURCE: 1 TERMINAL

FLICKERING
bodyHTML:
Grid engineers have traced a string of 340 micro-blackouts across a six-block stretch of San Francisco to a single residential terminal, in what the utility's own incident report describes as "a load signature we do not have a category for."

The outages, each lasting under two seconds, follow a distinctive pattern: a sharp draw spike, a brief system-wide flicker, then immediate stabilization — repeating, engineers say, "roughly whenever a particularly demanding prompt gets submitted." The terminal in question has not been publicly identified, though its billing address places it within a block of an apartment this publication has covered before.

"We've dealt with grow lights, crypto rigs, the occasional illegal data center. We have never had a single apartment unit request a load profile that looks like this. It looks like a whole building, not a person."
— Senior grid engineer, PG&E

The utility has installed a dedicated substation regulator on the block "as a precaution," and has quietly begun referring to the address internally by a code name, which this publication has agreed not to print at the utility's request.

Neighbors report the blackouts are brief enough to be a minor annoyance rather than a real disruption — mostly noticeable as a flicker in porch lights, timed, several residents note, suspiciously close to dinnertime.
